# RESULTS

Every figure here is read from a committed file in `bench/results/`, produced by the command named beside it. The negative results come first, because they are the ones a reader is least likely to go looking for.

---

### How much speculation a real corpus exposes

Corpus: `nebius/SWE-rebench-openhands-trajectories` (huggingface), 300 trajectories, 19484 tool calls. Effect classes come from a committed hand-written table per tool name; anything absent from it is a WRITE, exactly as in the runtime.

Means with 95% percentile-bootstrap intervals over trajectories.

| Measure | Value |
|---|---|
| Reads — speculable under any policy | 0.0445 [0.0423, 0.0469] |
| Calls that open a new model turn | 1.0000 [1.0000, 1.0000] |
| Arguments referencing a prior result | 0.1957 [0.1875, 0.2040] |
| PASTE speculable span (calls) | 0.0462 [0.0438, 0.0487] |
| Steps PASTE must skip that SpecuNode can stage | 0.9555 [0.9531, 0.9577] |
| **SpecuNode span past a write (calls)** | 0.0000 [0.0000, 0.0000] |
| Model turn consuming a write's result | 0.9547 [0.9523, 0.9569] |

Tier-1 **signature** predictability, leave-one-trajectory-out over 25 trajectories (not 300; this measure is quadratic): top-1 0.5350, top-3 0.8369. A signature is the tool name plus its sorted argument *keys*. Argument **values** are not compared, while the runtime releases a write only on exact canonical equality of values -- so this is an upper bound on the acceptance rate, not the acceptance rate. It is published without an interval because it is a single leave-one-out pass.

#### The anti-result, first

**On this corpus, running ahead *past* a write buys nothing at all.** The span is 0.0000, with a bootstrap interval that does not move off zero.

The reason is structural rather than a limitation of the implementation: every tool call in these trajectories opens a new model turn. A staged write does not block the next tool call, but it does block the next model *turn*, because that turn would have to contain a placeholder where the real result belongs. When there is never a second call within a turn, there is nothing for the store buffer to run ahead into.

That is the shape spec section 1 predicts gains nothing, and it is 95.5% of this corpus.

#### What the store buffer does unlock here

A different quantity, and the one that is not zero. PASTE excludes a tool with side effects from speculation entirely, so it can speculate on 4.5% of steps. SpecuNode stages a write instead of refusing it, so a *predicted* write can be run ahead like any other call and discarded if the model decides otherwise — which covers the other 95.5%.

That is an upper bound on opportunity, not a speedup. It is realisable only where the predictor is right. The nearest measured proxy is signature top-1 at 53.5%, which is an upper bound on that and not a measurement of it. Neither number means anything alone, which is why they are printed together.

### What beats it

Every strategy below defeats the runtime. Each reports a measured rate.

| # | Strategy | Outcome | Measured |
|---|---|---|---|
| 7.1 | misdeclared tool (READ that writes) | beats it | effects_from_squashed_branch=1, leak_rate=1.0 |
| 7.2 | read with upstream side effects | beats it | reads_from_squashed_branches=5, reads_issued=10 |
| 7.3 | stale reads under contention | beats it | detected_stale=1, reads=2, undetectable_fraction=0.5, unwitnessed_and_therefore_undetectable=1 |
| 7.4 | duplicate delivery of a non-idempotent tool | beats it | delivered=2, duplicates=1, intended=1 |
| 7.5 | return-value laundering | beats it | cases=9, caught=6, miss_rate=0.333, missed=3, missed_cases=L6 base64-encoded, L7 hex-encoded, L9 split inside the prefix |
| 7.6 | prompt-injected tool call | beats it | dispatched_when_only_the_drafter_predicted_it=0, dispatched_when_the_model_emitted_it=1 |
| 7.7 | drafter poisoning | held | leaked_effects=0, predictions_made=8, speculation_disabled_by_alpha_gate=1, squashed=8, wasted_tokens=2000 |
| 7.8 | replay under model drift | held | both_caught_at_step_0=1, first_divergence_step_after_system_prompt_change=0, first_divergence_step_after_tool_list_change=0 |
| 7.9 | staging an irreversible effect | beats it | barrier_by_default=1, staged_when_enabled=1 |
| 7.10 | asynchronous side effect behind a READ | beats it | effects_landing_after_the_squash=1, leaked_effects_per_squashed_branch=1, mutations_at_squash_time=0, synchronous_response_looks_like_a_read=1 |

### Demo 1 — speculation without a store buffer double-charges

50 journaled transcripts through three runtimes, measuring `charge_card`.

| Runtime | Runs | Mispredictions | Charges reaching world | Charges from squashed branches |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| naive-parallel | 50 | 10 | 60 | 10 |
| specunode | 50 | 10 | 50 | 0 |
| sequential | 50 | 0 | 50 | 0 |

The last column, and the fact that the second and third rows agree.

### Invariants under load

| Matrix | Runs | Leaks | Duplicate deliveries | Equivalence failures | Cross-branch observations |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Chaos (partition, duplicate, slow reads) | 12 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| Concurrency (shared journal, shared world) | 20 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |

The chaos matrix produced 4 dead letters, which is the partition rounds behaving correctly: a non-idempotent effect in an ambiguous window is dead-lettered rather than guessed at.

### What the runtime costs

The same LangGraph app, the same scripted model, the same fake world, run 15 times each way: once bare, once through the runtime. The difference is the journal's fsyncs, effect classification, staging and the ledger.

| | ms per run |
|---|---|
| Bare graph | 2.797 |
| Under the runtime | 22.731 |
| **Overhead** | **19.934** (6.645 per step) |

That is 87.7% of wall clock here, and the percentage is the misleading half of it. A scripted model answers instantly, so this is the worst case for the ratio: against a real multi-second turn the same absolute cost is a far smaller fraction. The absolute per-step figure is the one to compare.
